claim: Stable depletion of RalA or RalB by shRNA reduces by 40% the amount of secreted EVs in 4T1 cells
source: Stable depletion of RalA or RalB by shRNA reduces by 40% the amount of secreted EVs (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), with no impact on their average size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 1a and western blot validation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: RalA or RalB depletion has no impact on the average size of secreted EVs
source: Stable depletion of RalA or RalB by shRNA reduces by 40% the amount of secreted EVs (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), with no impact on their average size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: RBC8 and BQU57 are specific chemical inhibitors of Ral GTPases
source: RBC8 and BQU57, two previously described specific chemical inhibitors of Ral GTPases (Yan et al., 2014) significantly reduced EV secretion levels in mouse and human mammary tumor cell lines (4T1, MDA-MB231, D2A1, and MCF7 cells) as well as in two other cancer cell lines, human melanoma (A375) and pancreatic carcinoma (Panc1) cells (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Yan et al., 2014)

claim: RBC8 and BQU57 significantly reduce EV secretion levels in multiple cancer cell lines including 4T1, MDA-MB231, D2A1, MCF7, A375, and Panc1 cells
source: RBC8 and BQU57, two previously described specific chemical inhibitors of Ral GTPases (Yan et al., 2014) significantly reduced EV secretion levels in mouse and human mammary tumor cell lines (4T1, MDA-MB231, D2A1, and MCF7 cells) as well as in two other cancer cell lines, human melanoma (A375) and pancreatic carcinoma (Panc1) cells (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: The mechanisms by which RalA/B GTPases tune EV secretion levels are conserved throughout evolution
source: Together with evidence previously obtained in Caenorhabditis elegans (Hyenne et al., 2015), this demonstrates that the mechanisms by which RalA/B GTPases tune EV secretion levels are conserved throughout evolution and are notably at play in various cancer cell lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current study combined with previous work in C. elegans cited as Hyenne et al., 2015

claim: Endogenous RalA and RalB localize mostly within CD63-positive endosomal compartments (MVBs and late endosomes) and at the plasma membrane in 4T1 cells
source: Endogenous RalA and RalB localize mostly within CD63-positive endosomal compartments (MVBs and late endosomes), as well as at the plasma membrane (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1c

claim: GFP-tagged RalA and RalB localize both in late endosomal compartments positive for Lysotracker and at the plasma membrane
source: Similarly, GFP-tagged RalA and RalB localize both in late endosomal compartments positive for Lysotracker and at the plasma membrane (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1c

claim: In 4T1 cells, Ral GTPases localize both at biogenesis sites of microvesicles (plasma membrane) and exosomes (MVBs)
source: Therefore, in 4T1 cells, Ral GTPases localize both at biogenesis sites of microvesicles (plasma membrane) and exosomes (MVBs).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization data showing RalA/B at both plasma membrane and MVBs

claim: RalA or RalB depletion leads to a 40% decrease in the number of MVB per cytoplasmic surface in 4T1 cells
source: Strikingly, we found RalA or RalB depletion leads to a 40% decrease in the number of MVB per cytoplasmic surface in 4T1 cells (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), with no impact on the density of endolysosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: RalA/B depletion has no impact on the density of endolysosomes
source: Strikingly, we found RalA or RalB depletion leads to a 40% decrease in the number of MVB per cytoplasmic surface in 4T1 cells (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), with no impact on the density of endolysosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b

claim: RalA/B depletion has no significant effect on the late endosome-lysosome pathway
source: Further analysis of Lysotracker-positive compartments using FACS confirmed that RalA/B depletion has no significant effect on the late endosome-lysosome pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c

claim: Chemical fixation affects the morphology of endosomal compartments
source: However, since chemical fixation is known to affect the morphology of endosomal compartments, we took our EM analysis one step forward by implementing high-pressure freezing (HPF) of cells, which better preserves the ultrastructure of endosomes (Klumperman and Raposo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field (Klumperman and Raposo, 2014)

claim: High-pressure freezing better preserves the ultrastructure of endosomes compared to chemical fixation
source: However, since chemical fixation is known to affect the morphology of endosomal compartments, we took our EM analysis one step forward by implementing high-pressure freezing (HPF) of cells, which better preserves the ultrastructure of endosomes (Klumperman and Raposo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge (Klumperman and Raposo, 2014)

claim: Upon high-pressure freezing, RalA and RalB knockdown cells show a slight decrease in the number of ILVs per MVB surface
source: Upon HPF, we further observed a slight decrease in the number of ILVs per MVB surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d) that could be, in part, explained by a slight increase in MVB diameters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d

claim: RalA and RalB knockdown cells show a slight increase in MVB diameters upon high-pressure freezing
source: Upon HPF, we further observed a slight decrease in the number of ILVs per MVB surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d) that could be, in part, explained by a slight increase in MVB diameters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e

claim: Depletion of either RalA or RalB significantly reduces MVB number while the remaining MVBs are slightly bigger
source: In conclusion, depletion of either RalA or RalB significantly reduces MVB number, while the remaining MVBs are slightly bigger.
evidence: The claim summarizes the electron microscopy findings from both chemical fixation and high-pressure freezing experiments

claim: Both RalA and RalB control MVB homeostasis in breast mammary tumor cells
source: Overall, thorough EM analysis of intracellular compartments using both chemical fixation and HPF clearly demonstrates that both RalA and RalB control MVB homeostasis in breast mammary tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive electron microscopy data using two different fixation methods

claim: PLD1 and PLD2 are well-known targets of RalA and RalB
source: We decided to focus on phospholipases D (PLDs), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphatidic acid (PA), for three reasons: (1) PLD1 and PLD2 are two well-known targets of RalA and RalB (Jiang et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1998; Vitale et al., 2005), (2) PLD2 controls exosome secretion in breast cancer cells (Ghossoub et al., 2014), and (3) PLDs impact cancer progression (Bruntz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jiang et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1998; Vitale et al., 2005)

claim: PLD2 controls exosome secretion in breast cancer cells
source: We decided to focus on phospholipases D (PLDs), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphatidic acid (PA), for three reasons: (1) PLD1 and PLD2 are two well-known targets of RalA and RalB (Jiang et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1998; Vitale et al., 2005), (2) PLD2 controls exosome secretion in breast cancer cells (Ghossoub et al., 2014), and (3) PLDs impact cancer progression (Bruntz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ghossoub et al., 2014)

claim: PLDs impact cancer progression
source: We decided to focus on phospholipases D (PLDs), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphatidic acid (PA), for three reasons: (1) PLD1 and PLD2 are two well-known targets of RalA and RalB (Jiang et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1998; Vitale et al., 2005), (2) PLD2 controls exosome secretion in breast cancer cells (Ghossoub et al., 2014), and (3) PLDs impact cancer progression (Bruntz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Bruntz et al., 2014)

claim: Phospholipase D catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphatidic acid (PA)
source: We decided to focus on phospholipases D (PLDs), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphatidic acid (PA), for three reasons: (1) PLD1 and PLD2 are two well-known targets of RalA and RalB (Jiang et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1998; Vitale et al., 2005), (2) PLD2 controls exosome secretion in breast cancer cells (Ghossoub et al., 2014), and (3) PLDs impact cancer progression (Bruntz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the established enzymatic function of PLD

claim: Both PLD1 and PLD2 are expressed in 4T1 cells
source: We first verified that both PLD1 and PLD2 are expressed in 4T1 cells by RT-qPCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: PLD1 mostly localizes to endosomal compartments positive for RalA, RalB, and lysotracker
source: PLD1 mostly localizes to endosomal compartments positive for RalA, RalB, and lysotracker, whereas PLD2 mostly localizes to the plasma membrane (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: PLD2 mostly localizes to the plasma membrane
source: PLD1 mostly localizes to endosomal compartments positive for RalA, RalB, and lysotracker, whereas PLD2 mostly localizes to the plasma membrane (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: Inhibition of PLD1, but not PLD2, induces a 40% decrease in the number of MVBs per cytoplasmic surface in 4T1 cells
source: EM analysis of 4T1 cells revealed that inhibition of PLD1, but not of PLD2, induces a 40% decrease in the number of MVBs per cytoplasmic surface (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 2b

claim: Both PLD1 and PLD2 inhibitors reduce EV secretion levels in 4T1 cells
source: Further NTA analysis of treated cells showed that both inhibitors reduce EV secretion levels in 4T1 cells (Figure 2c), suggesting that both PLD isoforms regulate EV secretion potentially through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Both PLD isoforms regulate EV secretion potentially through distinct mechanisms
source: Further NTA analysis of treated cells showed that both inhibitors reduce EV secretion levels in 4T1 cells (Figure 2c), suggesting that both PLD isoforms regulate EV secretion potentially through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of PLD1 and PLD2 on MVB density despite both affecting EV secretion

claim: PLD1 inhibition fully phenocopies the effect of RalA/B GTPases depletion on both cellular density of MVBs and level of EV secretion
source: Importantly, PLD1 inhibition fully phenocopies the effect of RalA/B GTPases depletion, both on the cellular density of MVBs and on the level of EV secretion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of PLD1 inhibition with RalA/B depletion on MVBs and EV secretion

claim: In 40% of shRalA or shRalB cells, PLD1 is uniformly cytoplasmic instead of being endosomal
source: Confocal analysis revealed that in 40% of shRalA or shRalB cells, PLD1 is uniformly cytoplasmic instead of being endosomal (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging quantification shown in Figure 2d

claim: RalA/B depletion had no major impact on PLD2 localization at the plasma membrane
source: By contrast, RalA/B depletion had no major impact on PLD2 localization at the plasma membrane (also its trafficking might be altered) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c

claim: RalA/B GTPases are required for PLD1 localization on endosomes
source: This shows that RalA/B GTPases are required for PLD1 localization on endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PLD1 becomes cytoplasmic in RalA/B depleted cells

claim: RalA/B depletion significantly reduces the PA/PC ratio of secreted EVs
source: Importantly, RalA/B depletion significantly reduces the PA/PC ratio of secreted EVs (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic analysis data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Ral GTPases control PLD1 localization on MVBs, which is required for local PA accumulation and ultimately for MVB homeostasis and exosome secretion
source: Altogether, these results suggest that Ral GTPases control PLD1 localization on MVBs, which is required for local PA accumulation and ultimately for MVB homeostasis and exosome secretion (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental findings including PLD1 localization, PA/PC ratios, and MVB density

claim: High expression of either RalA or RalB is significantly correlated with reduced survival in breast cancer patients
source: Using a large cohort of breast cancer patients with metastatic progression from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), we found that high expression of either RalA or RalB is significantly correlated with reduced survival (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis from TCGA data shown in Figure 3a

claim: RalA and RalB are overexpressed in primary tumors from breast cancer patients with metastasis
source: Automated quantification of RalA/B expression levels by immunohistochemistry in primary tumors of breast cancer patients unraveled overexpression of both proteins in tumors from patients with metastasis (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 3b

claim: RalA depletion significantly increased tumor growth in orthotopic 4T1 mammary tumor model
source: First, RalA and RalB have antagonist effects on tumor growth measured in vivo over time and ex vivo after 41 days: while RalA depletion significantly increased tumors growth, RalB depletion induced the opposite effect when compared to control tumors (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor volume and weight measurements shown in Figure 3c

claim: RalB depletion significantly decreased tumor growth in orthotopic 4T1 mammary tumor model
source: First, RalA and RalB have antagonist effects on tumor growth measured in vivo over time and ex vivo after 41 days: while RalA depletion significantly increased tumors growth, RalB depletion induced the opposite effect when compared to control tumors (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor volume and weight measurements shown in Figure 3c

claim: Neither RalA nor RalB affected apoptosis in 4T1 tumors using caspase3 as a read-out
source: Neither RalA, nor RalB affected apoptosis, using caspase3 as a read-out (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by caspase3 measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b

claim: 4T1 cells depleted of RalA and RalB show increased growth rate in vitro
source: In contrast, 4T1 cells depleted of RalA and RalB show increased growth rate in vitro and a decreased proportion of cells in sub-G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c

claim: 4T1 cells depleted of RalA and RalB show a decreased proportion of cells in sub-G1 phase of the cell cycle
source: In contrast, 4T1 cells depleted of RalA and RalB show increased growth rate in vitro and a decreased proportion of cells in sub-G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d

claim: Increased proliferation rates were observed in vivo in the absence of RalA
source: A similar increase in proliferation rates was observed in vivo in the absence of RalA (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 staining quantification shown in Figure 3d

claim: Depletion of RalA favors in vivo tumor growth by enhancing 4T1 proliferation potential
source: Therefore, while depletion of RalA favors in vivo tumor growth by enhancing 4T1 proliferation potential, it is likely that additional non-cell autonomous factors are responsible for the decreased tumor growth observed upon RalB depletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of increased tumor growth and increased proliferation observed upon RalA depletion

claim: Additional non-cell autonomous factors are likely responsible for the decreased tumor growth observed upon RalB depletion
source: Therefore, while depletion of RalA favors in vivo tumor growth by enhancing 4T1 proliferation potential, it is likely that additional non-cell autonomous factors are responsible for the decreased tumor growth observed upon RalB depletion.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that RalB depletion decreases tumor growth without affecting proliferation

claim: RalA or RalB depletion in mammary tumors drastically reduced their metastatic potency to the lungs
source: We measured the number and the surface covered by metastatic foci in serial lung sections and observed that RalA or RalB depletion in mammary tumors drastically reduced their metastatic potency (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of lung metastases shown in Figure 3e

claim: The most dramatic reduction of metastasis was observed in the case of RalA depletion when compared to the tumor growth rate
source: When compared to the tumor growth rate, the most dramatic reduction of metastasis was observed in the case of RalA depletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of RalA depletion on tumor growth (increased) versus metastasis (decreased)

claim: Although RalA and RalB have antagonist effects on primary tumors, they both promote metastasis
source: These experiments show that although RalA and RalB have antagonist effects on primary tumors, they both promote metastasis.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings that RalA and RalB have opposite effects on tumor growth but similar effects on metastasis

claim: RalA or RalB expression levels have no effect on motility potential of 4T1 cells in 2D and 3D invasion assays
source: We performed 2D (Figure 3f) and 3D (Figure 3g) in vitro invasion assays and observed no effect of RalA or RalB expression levels on motility potential of 4T1 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing and 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 3f and 3g

claim: RalA/B promote metastasis of aggressive breast cancer cells non-cell autonomously by inducing pro-metastatic micro-environmental changes
source: Therefore, RalA/B seem to promote metastasis independently of cell invasion and are likely to promote metastasis of aggressive breast cancer cells non-cell autonomously by inducing pro-metastatic micro-environmental changes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RalA/B promote metastasis without affecting cell migration or invasion

claim: Depletion of RalA or RalB had no drastic effect on the soluble factors secreted by 4T1 cells
source: Depletion of RalA or RalB had no drastic effect on the soluble factors secreted by 4T1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by secretome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The secretion of WISP1/CCN4 is significantly decreased in shRalA/B cells
source: However, the secretion of one protein known to promote metastasis (Ombrato et al., 2019), WISP1/CCN4, is significantly decreased in shRalA/B cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by secretome analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Ombrato et al., 2019

claim: WISP1/CCN4 is known to promote metastasis
source: However, the secretion of one protein known to promote metastasis (Ombrato et al., 2019), WISP1/CCN4, is significantly decreased in shRalA/B cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ombrato et al., 2019)

claim: RalA and RalB are likely to enhance metastatic potency by promoting the secretion of EVs and possibly through WISP1/CCN4
source: Thus, RalA and RalB are likely to enhance metastatic potency by promoting the secretion of EVs and possibly as well through WISP1/CCN4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of RalA/B on EV secretion and WISP1/CCN4 levels

claim: Tumor EVs induce vascular permeability in the vicinity of tumors as well as in distant organs
source: Since tumor EVs are known to induce vascular permeability in the vicinity of tumors as well as in distant organs (Tominaga et al., 2015; Treps et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2014), we tested the capacity of RalA/B dependent EVs to promote endothelial permeability in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Tominaga et al., 2015; Treps et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2014)

claim: 4T1 EVs increase endothelial monolayer permeability in a dose-dependent manner
source: When added to a monolayer of endothelial cells, 4T1 EVs increased its permeability in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro permeability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e

claim: Endothelial monolayers become less permeable when treated with EVs derived from shRalA or shRalB cells compared to control EVs
source: Interestingly, endothelial monolayers became less permeable when treated with a similar amount of EVs derived from shRalA or shRalB cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro permeability assay comparing equal numbers of EVs from different cell types

claim: EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells fail to disrupt adherent and tight junctions by contrast to EVs derived from 4T1 control cells
source: Similarly, such EVs fail to disrupt adherent and tight junctions by contrast to EVs derived from 4T1 control cells (Figure 4b) suggesting that EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells have reduced pro-permeability abilities.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of VE-cadherin and ZO1 shown in Figure 4b

claim: EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells have reduced pro-permeability abilities
source: Similarly, such EVs fail to disrupt adherent and tight junctions by contrast to EVs derived from 4T1 control cells (Figure 4b) suggesting that EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells have reduced pro-permeability abilities.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RalA/B knockdown EVs fail to disrupt junctions and reduce permeability

claim: Depletion of RalA/B reduces secretion levels of EVs and leads to the secretion of EVs whose effect on vascular leakiness is hampered
source: Therefore, depletion of RalA/B reduces secretion levels of EVs and leads to the secretion of EVs whose effect on vascular leakiness is hampered.
evidence: The claim summarizes the dual effects of RalA/B on both EV quantity and quality

claim: Priming of lungs with control EVs significantly enhances lung metastasis over 14 days when compared to PBS
source: Priming of lungs with control EVs significantly enhances lung metastasis over 14 days when compared to PBS (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo metastasis priming experiment data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Priming of mouse lungs with EVs derived from Ral-depleted cells did not promote metastasis
source: In striking contrast, priming of mouse lungs with a similar number of EVs derived from Ral-depleted cells did not promote metastasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo metastasis priming experiment comparing different EV types

claim: RalA/B confer pro-metastatic functions to EVs, in addition to controlling their secretion levels
source: This key experiment demonstrates that RalA/B confer pro-metastatic functions to EVs, in addition to controlling their secretion levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that equal numbers of RalA/B-depleted EVs fail to promote metastasis

claim: 4T1 EVs mostly accumulate in the lungs, liver and brain 1 hour after injection
source: We found that 1 hr after injection 4T1 EVs mostly accumulate in the lungs, as well as the liver and brain (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo organ fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: The lungs, liver and brain are the main metastatic organs of 4T1 cells and breast carcinoma
source: These three organs are the main metastatic organs of 4T1 cells, and breast carcinoma, showing that the organotropism of 4T1 EVs mirrors the metastatic organotropism of their parental cells and further validates the relevance of our model to human pathology (Kaur et al., 2012; Lou et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kaur et al., 2012; Lou et al., 2008)

claim: The organotropism of 4T1 EVs mirrors the metastatic organotropism of their parental cells
source: These three organs are the main metastatic organs of 4T1 cells, and breast carcinoma, showing that the organotropism of 4T1 EVs mirrors the metastatic organotropism of their parental cells and further validates the relevance of our model to human pathology (Kaur et al., 2012; Lou et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing EV accumulation sites with known metastatic sites

claim: 4T1 EVs mostly accumulate in endothelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts of the lung parenchyma
source: Through a careful analysis of cell types that internalize EVs in these conditions, we observed that 4T1 EVs mostly accumulate in endothelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts of the lung parenchyma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of EV-positive cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: EVs derived from RalA- or RalB-depleted cells failed to efficiently reach the lungs
source: Importantly, EVs derived from RalA- or RalB-depleted cells failed to efficiently reach the lungs, even though similar amounts were injected in all conditions (Figure 4d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo organ fluorescence and lung section imaging shown in Figure 4d,e

claim: EVs derived from RalA- or RalB-depleted cells show reduced liver accumulation
source: Similar results were observed for EVs reaching the liver (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by liver fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: RalA/B control the pro-metastatic properties of EVs by tuning their ability to reach vascular regions and efficiently reach metastatic organs
source: Hence, we can conclude at this stage that RalA/B control the pro-metastatic properties of EVs by tuning their ability to reach vascular regions and local parenchyma and efficiently reach metastatic organs, thereby modulating the formation of a pre-metastatic niche.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the biodistribution experiments showing reduced organ targeting of RalA/B-depleted EVs

claim: EVs target specific vascular regions by first arresting at the surface of endothelial cells
source: We recently showed that EVs target specific vascular regions by first arresting at the surface of endothelial cells (Hyenne et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hyenne et al., 2019)

claim: Internalization of 4T1 EVs within endothelial cells is decreased after 1 hour when they originate from RalA/B-depleted cells
source: Using microfluidics, we found that internalization of 4T1 EVs within endothelial cells is decreased after 1 hr when they originate from RalA/B-depleted cells (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by microfluidics imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4f

claim: Endothelial arrest/internalization of EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells is significantly hampered in zebrafish embryos
source: Similarly, upon tracking of fluorescent EVs injected in the circulation of zebrafish embryos, we observed that endothelial arrest/internalization of EVs from RalA/B knockdown cells is significantly hampered (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by zebrafish imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4g

claim: RalA/B knockdown significantly reduces the adhesive properties of EVs to the endothelium
source: Altogether, these experiments suggest that RalA/B knockdown significantly reduced the adhesive properties of EVs to the endothelium, establishing a potential link with their failure to accumulate in mice lungs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced endothelial arrest/internalization observed in microfluidics and zebrafish experiments

claim: RalA/B GTPases control the pro-metastatic function of EVs by modulating their content
source: Furthermore, our results support a model in which RalA/B GTPases, in addition to promoting EV secretion, also control the pro-metastatic function of these EVs, likely by modulating their content.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional differences observed with equal numbers of EVs from different cell types

claim: A large proportion (30-50%) of the RNAs present in EVs from shRal cells differ from control EVs
source: We first analyzed the RNA content of EVs using RNAseq and found that a large proportion of the RNAs present in EVs from shRal cells were different from the control (30–50%) (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5a and Supplementary file 1

claim: GO terms associated with mRNA enriched in each EV type showed important differences in biological processes, molecular function, or cellular components
source: Accordingly, GO terms associated with mRNA enriched in each EV type showed important differences in biological processes, molecular function, or cellular components (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: EVs from shRalA cells showed an important increase in non-coding RNA compared to control or shRalB EVs
source: In addition, EVs from shRalA cells differed from control or shRalB EVs in the nature of the RNA they contain, as shRalA EVs showed an important increase in non-coding RNA (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA type analysis shown in Figure 5b

claim: RalA/B have a profound impact on the content of RNA in 4T1 EVs
source: Overall, this experiment reveals that RalA/B have a profound impact on the content of RNA in 4T1 EVs.
evidence: The claim summarizes the RNA sequencing findings showing extensive differences in RNA content

claim: 4T1 EVs contain a large number of proteins usually found in small EVs, including 77 of the top 100 proteins from Exocarta
source: As shown in Figure 5c and 4T1 EVs contain a large number of proteins usually found in small EVs (77 of the top 100 proteins from Exocarta are found in 4T1 EVs; Supplementary file 2), such as tetraspanins, integrins, ESCRT proteins or small GTPases, such as RalA/B themselves.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5c and Supplementary file 2

claim: Many proteins in 4T1 EVs are known to localize to endosomes, suggesting that some of these EVs are bona fide exosomes
source: Importantly, many of these proteins are known to localize to endosomes, suggesting that some of these EVs are bona fide exosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of endosomal proteins in the EV proteome

claim: No protein is exclusive to one type of EVs (control, shRalA, or shRalB)
source: Unexpectedly, comparison of the proteome of EVs secreted by RalA or RalB knockdown cells did not reveal major differences, as no protein is exclusive to one type of EVs.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry comparison of EV proteomes

claim: A small proportion of proteins showed differential expression levels between control and RalA/B knockdown EVs
source: Instead, a small proportion of proteins showed differential expression levels (Figure 5d; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry quantification shown in Figure 5d and Supplementary file 2

claim: EVs from control cells are closer to EVs from shRalB cells (97 proteins with differential expression) than to EVs from shRalA cells (217 proteins with differential expression) regarding their protein content
source: Regarding their protein content, we noted that EVs from control cells are closer to EVs from shRalB cells (97 proteins with differential expression) than to EVs from shRalA cells (217 proteins with differential expression).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry comparison showing different numbers of differentially expressed proteins

claim: Five proteins are over-expressed in EVs from shCtl cells compared to both EVs from shRalA and shRalB cells: CD146/MCAM, Clic4, Glypican 4, BDKRB2, and Abcg2
